title: Short Stuff: History of Spring Break
summary: Short Stuff episode on the history of spring break. The hosts open with banter about the song "Where the Boys Are," then trace spring break from early college weekend trips in the 1800s and the 1920s drinking shift, through the Great Miami Hurricane and Fort Lauderdale's Olympic-sized pool, the Colgate swim team's Florida training trips and the Elbow Room bar, to the 1958 Glendon Swarthout book "Unholy Spring" (retitled "Where the Boys Are") and the 1960 MGM film. They cover the growth of Fort Lauderdale, the shift to Panama City and Daytona Beach, MTV's live spring break broadcasts from 1986, the Atlanta Freaknick picnic and cruising from 1983, the Simpsons spring break episodes, Panama City Beach's 2015 crackdown on beach drinking, and alternative volunteer spring break programs.
topics: 1960 MGM film Where the Boys Are

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the short stuff episode with banter about the song Where the Boys Are and speak-singing.

segments.title: Origins: college trips and drinking before spring break
segments.summary: Chuck describes 19th-century college students taking spring weekend trips to hot springs and the coast, the rise of road trips and women's colleges in the early 20th century, and college drinking beginning in the early 1920s.

segments.title: Great Miami Hurricane and Fort Lauderdale pool
segments.summary: Josh describes the 1926 Great Miami Hurricane and Fort Lauderdale building an Olympic-sized pool to draw tourists. Chuck covers the 1928 pool, the Colgate swim coach who brought teams to train there, the 1938 College Coaches Swim Forum, and the Elbow Room bar at the Sea Breeze Hotel, which drew college students to Fort Lauderdale.
topics: Elbow Room bar Sea Breeze Hotel

segments.title: Transition to Where the Boys Are
segments.summary: A brief break and return to the Where the Boys Are theme, with a sung segment.

segments.title: Swarthout's book Unholy Spring and the 1960 film
segments.summary: In 1958 Michigan State English teacher Glendon Swarthout followed students on spring break in Fort Lauderdale and wrote the book Unholy Spring, retitled Where the Boys Are. MGM's 1960 film put Florida on the map and spring break grew to tens of thousands of students, nearing 400,000 in Fort Lauderdale by the mid-1980s.

segments.title: Spring break's darker side and hosts' experiences
segments.summary: Josh says spring break turned dangerous when older adults arrived. Chuck and Josh share memories of high school spring break trips to Panama City.
topics: Panama City high school spring break

segments.title: Florida crackdown and MTV's Daytona Beach broadcasts
segments.summary: Fort Lauderdale curbed drinking laws, and the mayor urged students to go elsewhere, so Florida towns like Panama City and Daytona Beach became destinations. MTV's live spring break broadcasts from 1986 featured the Beastie Boys and Starship in Daytona. The hosts also discuss Simpsons spring break episodes.

segments.title: Freaknick in Atlanta
segments.summary: In 1983 Black college students in Atlanta held a picnic called Freaknick, inspired by songs by Chic and Rick James. It grew into a large cruising event that lasted about a decade and clogged Atlanta's streets.

segments.title: Freaknick reaction, documentary, and cruising laws
segments.summary: Chuck discusses media portrayal of Freaknick and recommends the Hulu documentary Freaknick: The Wildest Party Never Told. Josh says new cruising laws broke up Freaknick. Panama City Beach became a spring break hub, and after a 2015 incident it banned drinking on the beach.
topics: Panama City Beach 2015 beach drinking ban

segments.title: Alternative spring break options
segments.summary: Chuck notes Panama City Beach's spring break now falls in March, and that many universities offer alternatives such as Habitat for Humanity volunteering and HIV advocacy programs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode with the show's sign-off and an iHeartRadio production credit.
